adds.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report on the Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act documents Ekiti State enforcement on the ground: on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; HRW reports she was beaten at least twice over the period and, unable to use Ekiti health services safely, travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment. The report also records a September 2014 arrest at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti — a gay man's third arrest, released after two days in detention by paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend — and a 2014 incident in which a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti. These are the state-specific beatings, arrests and bribe-payments that the record's summary previously had no Ekiti source to cite.

adds.title: Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe: The Impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act | Human Rights Watch
adds.summary: Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report documents the SSMPA's impact in Enugu State: Sharon, a bisexual woman from Enugu State, told HRW she married a male friend from high school in July 2015 under family and social pressure, saying 'For as long as I am in Nigeria, I will stay married.' An Enugu-based activist told HRW that 'the major challenge in Enugu State is the rate of HIV and STIs among members of the community' and that there are no clinics where gay men and men who have sex with men can access services without fear of harassment, forcing many to travel to Lagos and other states. This supplies the Enugu-specific social-coercion and healthcare-access findings absent from the record's existing sources.
